prompt: Ana types `go version` and the shell answers `bash: line 1: go: command not found`, with exit status 127. What does that tell her?
hint: 127 comes from the shell, not from Go.

choices.text: The archive is damaged and has to be downloaded again
choices.why: A damaged archive would leave a `go` that fails when it runs. Here nothing ran at all: the shell never found a file to start.

choices.text: The shell found no `go` in any directory on her `PATH`
choices.why: Right. 127 is the shell's code for a command it could not find; the fix is the two `export` lines in `~/.profile` and a fresh login.

choices.text: Go 1.27.1 refuses to run on Ubuntu 24.04
choices.why: Every transcript in the course ran Go 1.27.1 on Ubuntu 24.04. A refusal would come from Go itself, with its own message.

choices.text: `gcc` is missing, so the go command will not start
choices.why: Without `gcc` the go command starts and turns cgo off. The missing compiler shows up later, as the `-race` refusal.

prompt: On a machine where nobody set it, `go env CGO_ENABLED` prints `0`. What is the most likely cause?
hint: The section showed this value on a `PATH` with one program missing.

choices.text: The go command looked for a C compiler and found none
choices.why: Right. With no `gcc` on the path the go command quietly turns cgo off, and the race detector then refuses to build.

choices.text: Go 1.27.1 ships with cgo turned off by default on Linux
choices.why: On the lab machine, with `gcc` present, the same command printed `1`. The default follows the compiler.

choices.text: The module's `go.mod` asks for a newer release of Go
choices.why: That fails with a message naming the version `go.mod` requires. It has nothing to do with cgo.

choices.text: `~/go/bin` is missing from `PATH`
choices.why: That directory holds programs you built with `go install`. The C compiler lives in `/usr/bin`.

prompt: Why does the course recommend a virtual machine, rather than the Go Playground, to a student on Windows who cannot install Go directly?
hint: Think about what this course does around the program.

choices.text: The Playground runs a release older than 1.27.1
choices.why: The section gives no such reason. What it says is missing is the terminal.

choices.text: A virtual machine compiles Go faster than Windows itself does
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; a VM costs memory and disk while it runs.

choices.text: It has no terminal for builds, linters and profilers
choices.why: Right. The Playground runs one file and shows its output; everything this course types around that file has nowhere to go there.

choices.text: The Playground refuses any program that imports a package
choices.why: It runs programs that import the standard library; `hits` would compile there. It is the tooling around it that has no home.

prompt: The race detector refuses to build with `go: -race requires ___; enable it by setting CGO_ENABLED=1` when no C compiler is on the path.
hint: The feature that lets Go call C, and that the race detector relies on.

prompt: Ana runs `./args -n=3 "two words" feb.log`. What does `flag.Args()` return?
hint: The shell decided the word boundaries before the program started.

choices.text: `["two words" "feb.log"]`
choices.why: Right. The quotes told the shell that `two words` is one word; the flag package removed `-n=3` and left the rest.

choices.text: `["two" "words" "feb.log"]`
choices.why: That would be the list without the quotes. The quotes never reach the program, but the boundary they drew does.

choices.text: `["-n=3" "two words" "feb.log"]`
choices.why: That is `os.Args` without its first element. `flag.Args` is what is left after the flags are taken out.

choices.text: `["\"two words\"" "feb.log"]`, quotes and all
choices.why: The shell removes the quotes before the program starts; `os.Args` in the transcript shows no quote characters.

prompt: In `./args --n 3 jan.log -v`, why is `-v` still false?
hint: Look at where `-v` sits relative to the first word that is not a flag.

choices.text: Go only accepts flags that are written with a single dash
choices.why: `--n` in the same command was read as `-n`. One dash or two mean the same flag.

choices.text: A boolean flag needs `-v=true` to be set
choices.why: `./args -v -n 3 …` set it to true with the bare `-v`. The position is what changed.

choices.text: Parsing stopped at `jan.log`, so `-v` became an argument
choices.why: Right. The flag package reads flags from the front and stops at the first word that is not one; `-v` ended up in `flag.Args`.

choices.text: `--n` swallowed both `3` and `jan.log` as its value
choices.why: `-n=3` in the output shows `--n` took one word, `3`. `jan.log` is in `flag.Args`.

hint: Two of them stop the program inside `flag.Parse`.

pairs.right: a usage listing and exit status 2
a usage listing and exit status 0

right_distractors: an error from the shell and exit status 127

prompt: Your colleague's `genlog` prints a different first line from the lesson's for `-n 5` with the default seed. What is the reasonable conclusion?
hint: What makes two runs produce the same lines?

choices.text: Their terminal uses a different time zone
choices.why: `genlog` builds its times in UTC and formats them with `Z`; the time zone of the shell does not enter it.

choices.text: Random numbers differ from one machine to the next
choices.why: A PCG generator built from the same seed draws the same sequence on any machine; that is why the log is reproducible.

choices.text: Their program differs from the lesson's
choices.why: Right. Same seed, same program, same lines; a different line means a different list, a different order of draws or a different seed.

choices.text: `go run` recompiles and picks a fresh seed each time
choices.why: The seed is a flag with a default of 1; compiling again does not change it.

prompt: Why does `hits` keep the counting in `internal/tally` instead of in `main.go`?
hint: Lessons 2 to 4 change something and keep something else.

choices.text: Go requires a `main` package to stay under 100 lines
choices.why: There is no such rule. The split is a design decision, not a compiler limit.

choices.text: So three command lines in lessons 2 to 4 share it
choices.why: Right. Three command lines in lessons 2 to 4 sit in front of the same package, and `internal` keeps outsiders from importing it.

choices.text: A package under `internal` compiles faster
choices.why: `internal` changes who may import the package, not how fast it builds.

choices.text: The flag package refuses to run outside `main`
choices.why: `FlagSet` works in any package. `tally` keeps away from flags because it has nothing to do with a command line.

prompt: Each subcommand of `hits` builds its flags with `flag.NewFlagSet(name, flag.ContinueOnError)`. What does `ContinueOnError` change compared with the package-level `flag.Parse`?
hint: Who decides the exit code after a bad flag?

choices.text: `Parse` returns the error and the subcommand picks the exit code
choices.why: Right. The package-level functions exit by themselves; here `flagError` turns the error into 0 for `-h` and 2 for the rest.

choices.text: Unknown flags are ignored and parsing goes on to the next word
choices.why: `./hits top -n five` still failed with `invalid value`. Nothing is ignored; the error is returned instead of acted on.

choices.text: The usage listing is no longer printed on a bad flag
choices.why: The transcript shows the listing after `invalid value "five"`. `SetOutput` chose where it goes, not whether.

choices.text: Flags may appear after the file name as well as before it
choices.why: The FlagSet stops at the first non-flag word exactly like the package-level parser.

prompt: In the 20,000-line `access.log`, `hits count` reported 7,554 requests with status `200`. What percentage of the log is that, to the nearest whole number?
Which of these does the hand-written `hits` NOT do, and lesson 2's Cobra version adds? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section listed what was missing after the four mistakes.

choices.text: Suggest `count` when somebody types `cont`
choices.why: Yes. It printed `unknown command "cont"` and the usage, with no suggestion.

choices.text: Print `top`'s own help for `hits help top`
choices.why: Yes. `help` prints the general usage whatever follows it.

choices.text: Exit with status 2 on a flag value that does not parse
choices.why: It does that already: `./hits top -n five` ended in 2.

choices.text: Read the log from standard input when no file is named
choices.why: It does that already, in `summarise`.

prompt: Why does `hits` write `hits: open nope.log: no such file or directory` to standard error instead of standard output?
hint: Picture `hits top` at the start of a pipeline.

choices.text: Standard error is faster because it is not buffered
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given. The reason is what the next program in a pipeline would do with it.

choices.text: The shell colours standard error red
choices.why: Bash prints both streams the same way; the transcript shows no difference until one of them is redirected.

choices.text: The next program would take it for data
choices.why: Right. A report built from `hits top` would grow a row reading `hits: one file at most, got 2`.

choices.text: Go's runtime sends every string starting with the program's name there
choices.why: Nothing in the runtime routes by content; `run` writes to `stderr` because the code says so.

prompt: Match each situation with the exit code `hits` returns.
hint: 0 is success; the other two separate whose fault it was.

prompt: `./genlog -n 1000000 | head -1` left `genlog` with status 141. The shell reports a program killed by a signal as 128 plus the signal's number. Which signal number killed `genlog`?
hint: 141 minus 128.

prompt: A teammate moves the work into `main` and reads `os.Args` and `os.Stdout` directly, saying the four parameters of `run` were noise. What do they lose?
hint: How did `main_test.go` check the error paths?

choices.text: The ability to read standard input
choices.why: `main` can read `os.Stdin` as well as `run` can; the input still works.

choices.text: A test that runs the whole command line as a plain function
choices.why: Right. Without the parameters, the only way to check an exit code or a message is to build the binary and run it as a process.

choices.text: The exit codes, since `main` returns nothing
choices.why: `main` exits with `os.Exit`, as it does now; the codes survive the change.

choices.text: Speed, since passing writers through a function costs time
choices.why: An interface parameter costs nanoseconds per call; the argument for `run` is about testing, not speed.

prompt: After a pipeline runs, Bash keeps the exit code of every command in it in the array `${___[@]}`.
hint: The section printed `0 0` and `141 0` from it.

prompt: Put what happens in order when Ana runs `./hits top -n 2 access.log`.
hint: From the shell to the table.
items: the shell splits the line into words and starts `hits`
`run` reads `top` and passes the rest to `top`
`summarise` opens the file and `tally.Count` reads it
the `tabwriter` prints two rows and `run` returns 0

prompt: A nightly script runs `hits count "$f" > counts.txt` under `set -e`. One night the log has a malformed line 9,412. What happens?
hint: Follow the error message and the exit code separately.

choices.text: The script stops, and `counts.txt` is left empty
choices.why: Right. `Count` stops at the bad line, the message goes to standard error, the table is never written, and exit status 1 stops a `set -e` script.

choices.text: `counts.txt` holds the counts of the first 9,411 lines and the script goes on
choices.why: `hits` prints nothing to standard output when `summarise` fails, and status 1 stops the script.

choices.text: `counts.txt` contains the error message, because `>` captures the output
choices.why: `>` redirects standard output only, and the message is on standard error.

choices.text: The bad line is skipped and the counts cover 19,999 lines
choices.why: `Count` returns at the first line it cannot parse; it does not skip.

prompt: `go run ./tools/genlog -n 1000 -seed 3 | ./hits top -n 2` printed two paths. Where did `hits` get its input?
hint: No file name came after `-n 2`.

choices.text: From `access.log`, the file `hits` opens by default
choices.why: `hits` has no default file; with none named it reads standard input.

choices.text: From a temporary file the shell wrote `genlog`'s output into
choices.why: A pipe passes the bytes from one process to the other while both run; no file is made.

choices.text: From the second argument of `top`, which is `2`
choices.why: `2` is the value of `-n`. `flag.Args` was empty.

choices.text: From standard input, which the pipe connected to `genlog`'s standard output
choices.why: Right. With no file named, `summarise` keeps `in = stdin`, and the pipe made that `genlog`'s output.
